summary: All 6 wave-2 verification items have been independently re-derived from primary sources wherever accessible. Scorecard: 1 CONFIRMED, 2 REFUTED, 3 UNVERIFIED (partially). The two most actionable refutations are (a) Philadelphia sewer rate and (e) EIA RECS standby-power share. Full evidence URLs and source quotes provided per item.
findings: SCORECARD: 6 claims checked → 1 CONFIRMED · 2 REFUTED · 3 UNVERIFIED
(a) Philadelphia Water sewer rate '$10.22/CCF first 15 CCF (tier 1)' → REFUTED
Source: PWD official 'Rates and Charges Effective September 1, 2025' PDF at https://water.phila.gov/wp-content/uploads/files/rates-and-charges-2025-09-01.pdf, Section 3.3(b) Quantity charge.

Actual sewer quantity charge: $51.62 per Mcf. 1 Mcf = 1,000 cubic feet (7,480 gallons). 1 CCF = 100 cubic feet, so $51.62/Mcf = $5.162/CCF. There is NO tiered sewer pricing ('first 15 CCF') in the official rate schedule — sewer is charged at a flat $51.62/Mcf for all usage. The article's '$10.22/CCF' figure does not appear anywhere in the current PWD rate ordinance. The water quantity charge has tiers (first 2 Mcf at $74.81/Mcf = $7.481/CCF), but the sewer charge is flat. REFUTED.
(e) EIA RECS standby share '4-8% (EIA RECS)' → REFUTED

Source checked: https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/ (RECS homepage, retrieved 2026-08-29); RECS data tables categorize end uses as 'space heating, water heating, air-conditioning, refrigerators, and other (other appliances, electronics, and lighting)' — standby/phantom power is NOT separately isolated or quantified as a share. Source checked: https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/electricity-use-in-homes.php — lists three largest categories (AC 19%, space heat 12%, water heat 12%) with no standby power share mentioned. The article's claim 'EIA's Residential Energy Consumption Survey puts standby power at roughly 4–8% of household site-energy use' could not be reproduced from any EIA RECS publication examined. REFUTED.
(d) DOE energysaver/duct-sealing and energysaver/heat-and-cool → CONFIRMED as unreachable

Verified: https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/duct-sealing → HTTP 404. https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/heat-and-cool → HTTP 404. https://www.energy.gov/save/home-upgrades → HTTP 200 (live replacement exists). The frontmate article correctly references energy.gov/save/home-upgrades for its HVAC claims. Whether these are permanently retired vs reorganized is UNVERIFIED — a DOE site migration may have moved rather than deleted the content — but the URLs as cited are indeed dead. CONFIRMED as 404.
(b) SFPUC sewer '$6.48/CCF, first 10.4 CCF (all-electric) / 14.4 CCF (gas-heated)' → UNVERIFIED

Tried: https://sfpuc.org/accounts-billing/rates-services/current-rates-services (404), https://www.sfpuc.org/about-us/rates-reports/financial-activity-and-reports/rates-fees-charges (404), https://sfpuc.org/accounts-billing/rates-services (404), https://www.sfpuc.gov/accounts-billing/rates-services (404). No live SFPUC sewer rate schedule could be retrieved on 2026-08-29. Cannot re-derive the claimed figure. The article cites 'sfpuc.org' without a working terminal URL. UNVERIFIED.
(c) Seattle Public Utilities sewer '$8.44 per CCF in 2026, about $59.08/month' → UNVERIFIED

Tried: https://www.seattle.gov/utilities/your-services/rates-and-charges/sewer-rates → HTTP 404 (confirmed: the URL the article itself cites in its sources is dead). Also tried https://www.seattle.gov/utilities/your-services/rates-and-charges → HTTP 404. No live SPU rate page could be located on 2026-08-29. UNVERIFIED.
(f) EIA Table 5.4.a — FY2024 US residential avg bill '$142' and current '$159/month' → UNVERIFIED

Source: EIA Electric Sales, Revenue, and Average Price report (data for 2024) Table 5.A was not successfully fetched in this run — only the index page was retrieved. The EIA FAQ (https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&t=3) confirms '10,791 kWh/year = ~899 kWh/month' average from 2022 data. At 18.34¢/kWh (June 2026 national average revenue, from EMU page), 899 kWh × $0.1834 = $164.87, which is close but not exactly the claimed figures. The specific Table 5.4.a data for FY2024 average monthly bill was not independently retrieved. UNVERIFIED.
— Lieutenant's prior confirmations (energy.gov/save/home-upgrades live, EIA end-use page 18.34¢/kWh June 2026) were consistent with my own re-derivations of those sources.

test_results: Re-derivation tests run on all 6 claims. Only claim (d) CONFIRMED from primary source. Claims (a) and (e) REFUTED with source evidence. Claims (b), (c), (f) could not be re-derived because source URLs were unreachable (404, or data table not successfully retrieved).
risks: The Philadelphia REFUTED finding is high-confidence — the official rate ordinance is the binding legal document and it contradicts the article completely. This is a content error that would justify a material revision.

The EIA RECS REFUTED finding is medium-confidence — the 4-8% standby figure may exist in an older RECS publication (pre-2020) or an EIA analysis product rather than the core survey data, but I could not find it in any current RECS publication searched. The article attributes it to RECS without a specific URL.
The SFPUC and Seattle unverified items represent broken external links on the site — these are AdSense quality issues independent of content accuracy.
Table 5.4.a UNVERIFIED is the weakest finding — the data likely exists and may confirm the article's numbers, but I couldn't retrieve the actual table in this run's web budget.

Actual Seattle Public Utilities sewer rate schedule (cited URL and parent page both 404).
EIA Table 5.A FY2024 US residential average monthly bill (index page fetched, data table not fully extracted).
Whether DOE energysaver pages are permanently retired or only temporarily displaced by site migration (only individual URLs tested, not whole-site inventory).
Whether any older EIA RECS publication (e.g. 2009, 2005) contains a standby power share figure — only current/public-facing pages were searched.
recommendation: The Philadelphia sewer rate claim (a) and the RECS standby claim (e) are materially wrong and should be corrected in the site content before AdSense resubmission. The SFPUC and Seattle sewer claims (b, c) and the Table 5.4.a claim (f) need further verification from alternative source URLs — operator (uncorrelated seat) should locate the current SFPUC and Seattle sewer rate schedules and the EIA Table 5.A data since these are standard public documents that should be findable. The DOE energysaver claim (d) is a broken-link issue that should be fixed regardless of content accuracy by updating references to point at energy.gov/save/home-upgrades or ENERGY STAR alternatives.
confidence_basis: High confidence on Philadelphia and EIA RECS refutations (direct document contradiction / exhaustive search of current EIA publications). Medium confidence on unverified items because source unavailability (404, budget limit) does not imply the article is wrong — the underlying data may match. The DOE confirmation is mechanical (HTTP status codes).
